content: The Kaiser Richmond Field Hospital was the first hospital established under the Kaiser Permanente system. It is recognized as a historic site in Richmond, California, and is part of the Rosie the Riveter/World War II Home Front National Historical Park. As a component of this park, it is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The hospital provided medical services to the surrounding communities until 1995, when it was replaced by the Richmond Medical Center, a modern facility located in downtown Richmond. The original field hospital is now closed but remains at its original location in South Richmond along Cutting Boulevard. During World War II, more American workers lost their lives in industrial accidents on the home front than U.S. soldiers killed in combat, at least until the Battle of Normandy in June 1944. In the summer of 2007, preliminary bus tours were introduced, featuring a unique model where local residents shared their personal experiences from the wartime era, offering a deeper historical perspective on otherwise ordinary streets. Henry J. Kaiser, the owner of the Richmond Shipyards, recognized that a healthy workforce was essential to meet the wartime construction demands and deadlines. He implemented a groundbreaking concept of pre-paid medical care for workers, which soon extended beyond the workforce. For many workers, this was their first experience receiving medical attention. The hospital, sponsored by Kaiser’s Permanente Foundation, opened on August 10, 1942, under the direction of Medical Director Sidney R. Garfield. The Field Hospital was a mid-level facility within a three-tier medical care system. This system also included six well-equipped First Aid Stations located at individual shipyards and the main Permanente Hospital in Oakland, which handled the most critical cases. Together, these facilities served employees of the Kaiser shipyards who enrolled in the Permanente Health Plan, commonly referred to as the Kaiser Plan. This plan was one of the first voluntary pre-paid medical plans in the United States and a direct precursor to modern health maintenance organizations (HMOs) as defined by the federal HMO Act of 1973. Approximately 2% of all Richmond shipyard employees joined the plan, which was the first voluntary group plan in the country to combine group medical practice, prepayment, and substantial medical facilities on such a large scale. After the war, the health plan was expanded to include workers' families. By 1990, Kaiser Permanente had become the largest nonprofit HMO in the United States. Due to wartime material rationing, the Field Hospital was constructed as a single-story wood-frame structure in a simple modernist design. Initially intended as an emergency facility, it opened with only 10 beds. Subsequent expansions increased its capacity to 160 beds by 1944. The hospital operated as a Kaiser Permanente facility until its closure in 1995. Kaiser conducted its first medical research at the Field Hospital in 1942 and later at another site before discontinuing animal research entirely in 1958 in favor of correlational studies. The site and its parcel, officially known as the Nystrom Tract Addition, are now owned by Masjeed Al-Noor.
